11162-the-story-of-little-black-mingo:
The author of The Story of Little Black Sambo wrote this short picture tale, The Story of Little Black Mingo. Little Black Mingo, a little girl with no father or mother, lives with a horrid cross old woman called Black Noggy, who scolds her daily and sometimes beats her with a stick.

Sent to the river with a chatty for water, Mingo meets a horrible big Mugger, a crocodile, who pokes his nose through the chatty's bottom and threatens to eat her up. She runs, and the broken chatty round his neck catches his paws, so he cannot overtake her. Black Noggy, furious, sends her with the dhobi's great chatty, and later a mongoose eats the Mugger's eggs while he sleeps curled around them. The tale follows Sambo's pattern of a small child outwitting a predator.
11991-po-no-kah-an-indian-tale-of-long-a:
Mary Mapes Dodge's 1903 tale Po-No-Kah, an Indian tale of long ago, opens with the Hedden family and a reflection on pioneer hardship. Readers in comfortable country homes, Dodge writes, find it hard to conceive the trials of settlers who faced hostile Indians in every direction during the last century and for many years after.

The story follows a search, as Neighbor Hedden hurries along a bank with new thoughts. Two children, Rudolph and Kitty, treated almost with kindness by their captors, fed well and given soft deer-skins at night. Dodge, editor of St. Nicholas magazine, writes for young readers, softening a captivity tale with attention to children's fear, playfulness, and resilience.
12895-capt-w-f-drannan-chief-of-scouts-a:
Captain William F. Drannan told this 1910 sequel to Thirty One Years on the Plains as his own story of piloting emigrant and government trains across the wild West. Illustrated by E. Bert Smith, it follows wagon trains, Indian attacks, hunting camps, and nights of dancing after fresh meat, with Carson as a fellow figure. Twelve chapters carry the tale.

A camp scene, where Jim orders a captured animal tied up lest it kill someone, shows the plain, boastful voice of the old scout. Drannan's tales mix fact, tall talk, and frontier detail. The book appeals to readers of western memoir who enjoy a scout's yarns at full stretch.
14077-a-frog-he-would-a-wooing-go:
Randolph Caldecott's picture book A Frog He Would A-Wooing Go retells the old nursery song in verse and pictures. Froggy sets off in an opera hat, heigho says Rowley, whether his mother lets him or not. He meets a rat, visits pretty Miss Mousey, and sings rowley-powley, gammon and spinach as refrain. Illustrations pace each stanza.

Miss Mouse sings a song she just made when Froggy catches cold. Later, crossing a silvery brook, a lily-white duck gobbles Froggy up. The song ends there, with the familiar chorus closing the tale. Caldecott's pictures made the book a nursery classic. It suits young children and lovers of illustrated songs.
1425-el-verdugo:
Balzac's short, grim tale is set in the Spanish town of Menda during the Peninsular War. At midnight a young French officer waits on a terrace. A Spanish family faces a terrible sentence: one of its own must carry out the execution of its kin, or all will die.

Told in a few taut pages, the story weighs honour, family duty, and the cruelty of war, and its ending lands with cold force. It is one of Balzac's starkest sketches, a brief study of what occupation and revenge demand of ordinary people caught between armies.
15173-pictures-of-jewish-home-life-fifty:
Hannah Trager's pictures of Jewish home life fifty years ago recall Jerusalem households of an earlier generation, with a prefatory letter by Leo Jung. Chapters cover arrival in Jerusalem, Purim, baking matzos, Lag B'Omer, the Sabbath, the succah, charity, and weddings. A glossary and four plates aid readers.

Trager writes with reverence for parents and custom, opening on a Friday afternoon as a family washes and dresses for synagogue. Her sketches preserve festival, school, and home ritual in warm detail. Readers interested in Jewish life in old Palestine will find the book tender, vivid, and instructive.
17429-the-story-of-dago:
Annie Fellows Johnston, author of the Little Colonel books, published this children's tale in Boston in 1900, with pictures by Etheldred B. Barry. Dago, kept in a small attic room while the children are away at school, slips out of the window and down the lightning rod to talk with a mirror-monkey. The whole book is framed as the stories Dago tells that toy, one for each day of a week.

Monday's tale opens the set, and each following day brings a fresh story, from a swing-rope bell and a fountain rescue to a funeral and a parting. The final chapter bids the mirror-monkey farewell. Young readers get a gentle, day-by-day storybook built on a toy's secret life when the house is quiet.
18606-the-camp-fire-girls-in-the-maine-w:
Hildegard G. Frey published this Camp Fire Girls tale at New York in 1916 with A. L. Burt. It follows the Winnebago group at a Maine lake camp, where Sahwah the Sunfish watches from a diving tower for the steamer Bluebird bearing a new girl, Gladys. Migwan, Hinpoha, and the rest wait with spyglass, sheet signals, and a treehouse Crow's Nest.

Talk of affinities, freckles, and star reading fills the opening, with lake swims, washing, and camp chores close behind. Frey writes in a sunny, chummy style for girls. The book is a light summer camp story from the Camp Fire era.
19730-warwick-woodlands-things-as-they-w:
Frank Forester wrote this sporting memoir of the Warwick woodlands as they were twenty years before, opening on a fine October evening in New York. The narrator reunites with his old friend Henry Archer, a staunch fellow and keen sportsman, after ten years apart.

Their talk ranges from Canadian log huts to tigers and arrack punch abroad, then turns to homeward rides on bright Sabbath mornings, full of mirth and good feeling. Forester's book is a fond record of field sports and friendship in a younger America. A grizzled local bets drinks on the day's deer, staking his own musket against Harry's rifle.
20385-some-three-hundred-years-ago:
Some Three Hundred Years Ago, published in 1922, looks back to the first years of settlement on the New England coast. Long before white settlers came, Native people camped by a fresh spring close to salty shores. The spot lay some three miles from the sea.

The same spring and shore later drew white settlers to build there. The story follows that change of hands and the hard early days of the newcomers. It gives young readers a grounded picture of how a coastal settlement began, and of the people who were there before it.
20579-the-frog-who-would-a-wooing-go:
The Frog Who Would A-Wooing Go retells the old nursery tale of a frog's courtship for young readers. It begins in proper storybook style. On the quiet, sedgy bank of a stagnant pool, under the shadow of rank reeds and bulrushes, sat two frogs in earnest talk.

The two had retired from the shoal sporting in the water. The elder frog advises the younger, who is set on going a-wooing. The tale follows the famous song: the frog's visit, the mouse, and the wedding plans that end in confusion. Picture-book versions like this one kept the rhyme in the nursery.
23121-our-little-lady-six-hundred-years-:
A west door frames the past in Our Little Lady, Six Hundred Years Ago. The narrator warns how strange that world would look to modern eyes. The Dark Ages earned their name, she says, in ways the present can barely grasp. She invites readers out through the west door to picture the scene six centuries back.

Through that doorway the book leads young readers into a medieval childhood. Emily Holt specialized in such guided descents into earlier centuries, castles, convents, and manners included. Her little lady lives the history rather than reciting it. The framing device, a modern narrator picturing the scene, keeps the strangeness honest. It is a child's tour of the Middle Ages with a story for a vehicle.
23371-blown-to-bits-the-lonely-man-of-ra:
R. M. Ballantyne built this tale around the Krakatoa blast, with much of the action in the forests of Java and Sumatra and on the seas around them. Van der Kemp, a lone settler who made his home on an island of the Krakatoa group, anchors the story, travelling far in a small canoe built for rough weather.

Forest life, island homes, and native helpers give the tale its colour, while the great eruption brings ruin, flight, and feats of seamanship. Ballantyne, drawing on the lore of Kingston and Fenn, keeps the perils close and the pace brisk. Readers get a stirring account of a world shaken by nature, and of men who meet disaster with courage, skill, and care for each other.
2523-the-memoirs-of-victor-hugo:
Victor Hugo left these memoirs as a mix of history and personal recall, covering French life from the coronation at Rheims in 1825 through the revolution of 1848. Hugo writes as both witness and actor, moving from royal courts to theaters, the Academy, and the Chamber of Peers.

The pages hold sketches of kings, actors, and deputies, scenes of street fighting, and quiet moments in prison and at home. Readers meet Lamartine, Thiers, and Louis Philippe through Hugo's sharp eye, and they see how a poet became a public voice. The book offers an insider's tour of a century of French upheaval, told by one of its loudest minds.
2547-half-a-life-time-ago:
Elizabeth Gaskell sets this tale in a Westmoreland dale. Susan Dixon, a single woman of property, farms some thirty or forty acres there. She also holds a sheep walk up to the wild fells above Blea Tarn. In local speech she is a stateswoman, a freeholder in her own right.

Susan's steady life breaks when Michael Hurst, the man she once loved, returns changed by drink and ruin. Gaskell follows her pride, her pity, and her hard choice with deep sympathy. The story is a quiet tragedy of love outliving youth, and a portrait of a strong woman holding her ground.
25719-the-privateer-s-man-one-hundred-ye:
Captain Marryat writes The Privateer's Man One Hundred Years Ago, in a Leipzig Tauchnitz edition of 1846 sanctioned for continental circulation. The book presents extracts from the log of a privateer's man, addressed to a respected madam at her request.

Marryat transcribes journal portions from his younger days without altering a word, so readers learn his feelings then, not his thoughts now. Cruises off Hispaniola, capture of a French ship, and a nocturnal attack on a rich planter's dwelling, repulsed with loss, open a sea tale of privateering in wartime. Marryat writes in a sailor's journal voice.
26153-the-last-of-the-legions-and-other-:
Arthur Conan Doyle's volume of thirteen historical tales, gathered from stories first printed between 1900 and 1922, ranges across the ancient world and beyond. The title story follows the last Roman legions. Other tales cover a last Punic galley that refuses capture and the coming of the Huns. Further tales treat an iconoclast, the giant Maximin, and a silver mirror with strange powers.

Each story stands alone, mixing battle, sea adventure, and touches of the uncanny, and each turns on a single bold act or twist of fate. Readers who know Doyle only through Sherlock Holmes will find his gift here too. These are swift, vivid yarns set in far-off times, told with the same clear pace as his detective fiction.
27422-through-the-malay-archipelago:
Emily Richings, author of Sir Walter's Wife and In Chaucer's Maytime, published this travel book in London with Henry J. Drane. Her prologue says the traveller who reaches the palm-girt shores of Ceylon enters a new range of thought and feeling, and the book follows that promise eastward through the islands.

Java brings Batavia, Buitenzorg, Djokjacarta, Boro-Boedoer, and Sourabaya. Celebes brings Makassar, the Minahasa, and Gorontalo. Then come a glimpse of Borneo, the Moluccas with Ternate, Ambon, and Banda, Sumatra with a view of Krakatau, and Penang. Richings writes warmly of tropical scenery and island life, and the journey still reads as an engaging tour.
28679-forgotten-tales-of-long-ago:
E. V. Lucas selected Forgotten Tales of Long Ago, with illustrations by F. D. Bedford, for Wells Gardner, Darton and Company of London. The fourth impression appeared in July 1931, gathering old children's stories that had slipped from print. Its motto looks backward to tales of old simplicity, heard in a mother's voice.

Contents include Dicky Random, Jemima Placid, Two Trials, Prince Life by G. P. R. James, and the Farm-Yard Journal by the Aikins. Maria Edgeworth's Waste Not, Want Not, Jacob Abbott's Malleville's Night of Adventure, and Dickens's Captain Murderer join them. Readers get a treasury of moral tales, rescued rather than rewritten.
30824-the-rushton-boys-at-treasure-cove-:
Spencer Davenport wrote this boys' adventure book, published by Whitman in Racine, Wisconsin, with a 1916 copyright held by George Sully and Company. It is one of the Rushton Boys series, after the boys at Rally Hall and in the saddle, where they met the ghost of the plains. Here the subtitle promises Treasure Cove and the missing chest of gold.

Chapter one, The Coming Storm, opens on a boat with Fred Rushton, his younger brother Teddy, and Lester Lee at the tiller. A great bank of cloud climbs the sky, and Fred warns that more than a capful of wind is in it, while the boys are a long way from home. Davenport mixes sailing, weather, and treasure hunting in the wholesome adventure style of his day, for young readers who love a hunt for gold.
3107-as-we-go:
Warner collects twenty-eight short studies of American life in this volume. Titles range from the president and the newspaper-made man to the electric way and the art of idleness. Other pieces ask if a husband may open his wife's letters, or weigh climate and happiness. A leisure class, a deadly diary, and the whistling girl sit side by side.

Each piece is brief and witty, built to catch a habit or a type in a few pages. Together they form a social notebook of the age. They record what amused, annoyed, and puzzled a keen watcher of manners, and how lightly a skilled essayist could touch a subject and still leave a mark.
31502-two-indian-children-of-long-ago:
Frances Lilian Taylor's Two Indian Children of Long Ago, published by the Beckley-Cardy Company of Chicago with copyright in 1920 and illustrated by L. Kate Deal, is a children's book about Native American life before European settlement. Its contents include "The First Americans," "The Wild-Rice Indians," and "Stories and Story-Tellers." Taylor, author of the Adventures in Storyland readers, writes for schoolchildren in simple, vivid prose.

The book follows two children through daily life: food gathering, story telling, and the customs of their people. Its aim is to teach respect and curiosity about the first Americans. Modern readers will read its period language with care, but its intent, to present Native children as the center of their own story, marks it as a humane schoolbook of its time.
32203-the-land-of-long-ago:
Eliza Calvert Hall's The Land of Long Ago was published in Boston by Little, Brown and Company in 1909. It gathers Kentucky stories in dialect. Hall, author of Aunt Jane of Kentucky, dedicated the book to Margery, Alexander, Thomas, and Cecilia. Drawings by G. Patrick Nelson and Beulah Strong accompany the text, with a frontispiece showing a picture of Henrietta's house, offered to a child.

Its nine chapters run from A Ride to Town and The House That Was a Wedding Fee. They continue through The Courtship of Miss Amaryllis and Aunt Jane Goes A-Visiting to The Marriage Problem in Goshen. An Eye for an Eye, The Reformation of Sam Amos, In War Time, and The Watch Meeting complete the set. Readers get a nostalgic, dialect-voiced portrait of Kentucky country life, courtship, marriage, and war, as remembered from long ago.
32340-the-o-donoghue-tale-of-ireland-fif:
Charles Lever's novel, published in Dublin in 1845, is subtitled a tale of Ireland fifty years ago, placing its action in the late eighteenth century. Dedicated to John Wilson, professor of moral philosophy at Edinburgh, it opens in Glenflesk, a wild valley winding between Macroom and Bantry Bay. Lever describes rugged mountains, granite slopes, and heath-bell colour as the perfect picture of Irish scenery.

From that valley the story follows the O'Donoghue family and their neighbours through the troubles of their time. Lever, writing as an Irish novelist of the 1840s, looks back to an age of landlords, tenants, and political strain. Readers get landscape, local character, and a historical romance rooted in Kerry country and its people.
32508-the-blind-lion-of-the-congo:
Elliott Whitney's Blind Lion of the Congo, copyrighted in 1912, follows Burton St. John, a seventeen-year-old boy of New Britain, Connecticut, whose father makes automobiles. At dinner, Mr. St. John asks what Burton has on for the night. Burton, sturdy but pale from hard study, answers with a frat meeting and a last history paper, while his parents watch with a hint of anxiety. An amazing proposal soon carries him far from school.

Chapters follow Critchfield interviewed, a decision, outfitting, the Congo, the mark, Critch's rhino, and Captain Mac suspected. White pygmies, a sacred ankh, and Mvita saving Burt's life lead onward. A pygmy village and a sacred lion follow, then an ivory zareba, a diary, a raft, and a run down the Makua. Whitney writes a boys' adventure of Africa, hunting, and river travel, with period views to read critically today.
32538-the-tower-of-dago:
Maurus Jókai's Tower of Dago, published in London in 1899 with illustrations by A. M. Bishop, opens with a strange tower rising from the sea near the Gulf of Finland. Passengers on a steamer from Stralsund see the object project high out of the water, and seamen call it the Tower of Dago. An old, wealthy Englishman once asked a captain what it would cost to examine the ruin close at hand, and received a blunt answer about his shrivelled skin and dried bones.

The tower, built on the outermost point of a rocky promontory of a great island, has escaped art galleries only because it cannot be brought before a painter's easel. Contents promise a return to the sea, an observatory, a sorcerer, a famine, compensation, a meeting, and reconciliation, with a minster bell, weakness, a severed cord, and nemesis.
34780-splores-of-a-halloween-twenty-year:
Alexander Dick published Splores of a Halloween, Twenty Years Ago at Woodstock, Canada West, in 1867. The preface explains that the verses were sent to compete for a prize offered by the Montreal Caledonian Society for the best poem on Halloween. They were not successful.

Dick publishes anyway, choosing to appeal from the judges' award to the decision of the public. The judges, by their own statement, weighed suitability for recitation at a public festival as heavily as literary merit. That rule, unstated in the invitation, excluded poems like his. Readers get a Scottish-Canadian grievance in verse and prose, and a Halloween poem judged twice.
35877-group-psychology-and-the-analysis-:
Sigmund Freud wrote Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego, a study of how crowds change minds. James Strachey turned the book into English for its press. The International Psycho-Analytical Press issued it in London in nineteen hundred twenty two. The German text had come out in Vienna one year prior.

A lone man thinks and acts one way when left to himself. Set him in a crowd and he shifts in strange ways at once. Le Bon’s famed book on crowds gives Freud his launch point. Suggestion and love ties then bear the weight of his case. The Church and the Army stand as two made groups. Sameness with the leader forms the core bond he finds. Love, trance, and the herd urge fill the late chapters. The primal horde of old myth ends his chain of thought.
36958-a-child-of-the-jago:
A Child of the Jago is a tale of the slums by Arthur Morrison, the hand of a famed set of mean street tales. The host print is the third form of the book. It was put out at London in eighteen ninety seven. The book is sworn to a church man of a poor ward of the east end. A stern quote from an old seer stands past the sworn leaf.

That quote wails on false seers who sing of peace where no peace is. It tells of a wall daubed with weak stuff, and of the storm that will rend it. A sketch plan of the old ward stands at the front. The tale opens past the mid of a warm night in the Old Jago. The tight street was the more black for the strange sky.
37712-the-crime-of-the-congo:
The Crime of the Congo, by Conan Doyle, was published in New York in 1909. Doyle, author of The Great Boer War, sets out how the Congo Free State came to be founded. He then traces how the state grew, and how its system worked, in chapter after chapter.

Heads name the first fruits of the system, and then further fruits. A section gives voices from the darkness. Consul Roger Casement report is treated at length, and so is King Leopold own commission and its report. Catholic testimony, the evidence to date, and the politics follow. Doyle closes with answers offered to Congo pleas, and with solutions. Readers get a famous public case against a colonial regime, built on reports and witness words.
39061-samba-a-story-of-the-rubber-slaves:
Herbert Strang tells a tale of the Congo rubber trade in a boys' book with pictures by William Rainey. The book first appeared in 1906 and is here in a second edition of 1908. A Congo proverb heads the title page, warning that rubber is death.

The story opens with Samba lying face down on yellow sand as the white man comes to his country. Chapters bring night alarms, blood brotherhood, a trip with a crocodile, and a revolt at Ilola. A foe named Elbel, his barrels, his blockade, and the chicotte whip drive the darker side of the plot. Samba goes missing and returns, and the tale ends with a break for liberty. Young readers get adventure with a clear view of forced labor's cruelty.
39255-the-fire-gods-a-tale-of-the-congo:
Fire Gods is a tale of the Congo by Captain Charles Gilson, pictured by George Soper. The London edition came from the office of a boys' paper. A list of the author's other tales stands at the front. Among them are tales of submarines, spies, and a race round the world. Chapter one is set at an explorers' club, chapter two on the Kasai river.

The club itself no longer exists, the tale begins. A tea shop in Old Bond Street stands in its place today, wedged between a milliner's and an art shop. Towards the end of the last century the club stood there in its prime, the narrator recalls. A cover scene shows a man seized from behind as he leans to examine a rock face. The contents promise a tale of travel and danger in central Africa.
40699-a-childhood-in-brittany-eighty-yea:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick wrote this book of a youth in Brittany of eighty years past, printed in 1919. Paul de Leslie drew its cuts. Its small sheaf of young thoughts was put in one set from many talks, in her own tongue, with an old friend from France. The names of her kin have been changed, by her wish. The list of parts names the stops of that youth.

Quimper and a dear grand dame stand at the head. A fête at a place named Ker-Eliane, an old house at Landerneau, and aunts and dames of the land fill the mid parts. A marquis has his part, and a feast of the Church at Folgoat has its own. The death of the grand dame and the trip out of Brittany close the book.
4384-the-lost-word-a-christmas-legend-of:
Henry Van Dyke wrote this Christmas legend of Antioch, fifteen hundred years ago, and published it in New York in 1898. It opens in the dusk of Christmas morning, as young men call their fellow student Hermas from his lodging. They have nearly finished two years of study for the church, and they cry that Christ is born and peace is with them.

The contents follow Hermas through poverty, a Christmas loss, parting without farewell, and love in search of a word. Riches without rest and great fear give way to recovered joy. Van Dyke's legend is a gentle parable about losing and finding the word that makes faith live.
45066-mrs-leary-s-cow-a-legend-of-chicag:
C C Hine's Mrs Leary's Cow, printed at New York in 1872 and presented by the Black River Insurance Company of Watertown, turns the Chicago fire into a cumulative comic ballad. A photograph card of the cow, sold after the fire, carries the tale on its back. Mrs Leary of De Koven Street went to her barn with a lamp on the night of October the eighth, and the cow kicked it over.

The verses build in the manner of the house that Jack built. Each new stanza adds the blasted city, the frame range of northern pine, and the gloomy insurance company. Every stanza ends by swearing at the cow with the crumpled horn that set fire to the barn.
46243-divine-authority-or-the-question-w:
Divine Authority, or the question was Joseph Smith sent of God, is a tract by Orson Pratt. Pratt was one of the twelve apostles of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The pamphlet opens with a tea visit in Liverpool in its first lines. Pratt and his wife were kindly invited to take tea with a town gentleman.

That host, though not of their church, was sincerely enquiring after the truth with his family. They seemed convinced on the chief features of the doctrine, he reports of the visit. They wished to extend their search still further in that talk. Pratt hopes their research may end in full conviction of the truth he preaches. A message revealed from heaven, a savor of life or death, is his claim for it.
46500-ford-of-h-m-s-vigilant-a-tale-of-t:
Ford of the Vigilant is a naval adventure novel by Jeans, a staff surgeon in the Royal Navy. Blackie published it at London in 1910. William Rainey illustrated the tale of the Chusan Archipelago. Jeans had written a midshipman story before it, and this book follows its lines. The preface says the proof sheets went to messmates for correction. Technical errors were weeded out by men of different branches.

Practically all the characters are drawn from life, Jeans adds. The cruisers and gunboats in the operations are real ships under altered names. Dick Ford goes to sea in the first chapter. The loss of Lieutenant Travers and Ford's first command follow. The Vigilant sails, fights, and lands a party in China seas. Ford saves an old shipmate's life near the end. Jeans aimed at an accurate picture of service life in wartime.
4757-the-long-ago:
Jacob William Wright wrote The Long Ago as memories, with an epigraph from II Esdras bidding a man weigh fire, measure wind, or call again the day that is past. Its contents run from The Garden and The River, through Christmas and Butter, Eggs, Ducks, Geese, to The Sugar Barrels and Jimmy, the Lamplighter. Flies, Autumn Leaves, Getting in the Wood, and Grandmother follow, closing with When Day is Done.

The opening finds the narrator lingering at an office window alone in the early evening. Street sounds surge up: the hoarse voice of the city, clanging trolley cars, rumbling wagons, and familiar cries. Buildings pour forth their tide of labourers into clogged arteries at the home-going hour. He leans against the window frame, looking across myriad roofs, while world-weariness touches his temples with grey. Readers get a wistful book of boyhood remembered from middle age.
49307-c-a-coey-s-school-of-motoring-1424:
Coey's School of Motoring at Michigan Avenue, Chicago, presents its lessons in a course book copyrighted in 1912, compiled by Coey, the school's president. A picture shows racer Barney Oldfield beating Coey's Tornado by six inches at the Saint Louis fair grounds. The school claims to be the only one actually building automobiles.

An address to the student argues that chauffeurs earn good pay, hold steady demand, and enjoy their employers' trust, some rising to wealth with a patron's help. The school's object is to train young men as expert chauffeurs, repairmen, demonstrators, salesmen, and garage managers. Coey, twelve years in the trade, says country boys match city lads in ambition but lack their chances, and his course means to supply them.
49357-outlines-of-mormon-philosophy-or-t:
Outlines of Mormon Philosophy is a work of theology by Wilson, issued at Salt Lake City in 1905. Its subtitle calls it the gospel's answers to the questions of life. Those answers came through the prophet Joseph Smith, it holds. Wilson had written the life of David Patten before. The book is dedicated to Smith's memory. Smith gave his life for these truths, Wilson says.

The preface warns that the work is made for study. A hasty reader will find it short and dull, he grants. A studious one will find it vast. Each man builds his own system of thought, Wilson holds. Better to build on what the Lord has shown. The church's First Presidency helped with criticism. The book maps Mormon belief in outline form.
50282-the-speedwell-boys-and-their-racin:
Roy Rockwood wrote a boys' novel copyrighted in 1913, subtitled a run for the golden cup. Rockwood also wrote the Dave Dashaway and Great Marvel series. A front picture shows two automobiles coming through close together. Contents open with the manoeuvres of Maxey and Dan Speedwell at his best.

A mystery of a maroon car and a bank robbery follow. Chapters name a hand in the dark, thieves in the night, and Josiah Somes on the warpath. The boys take a hot trail toward Karnac Lake. An endurance test fills the later chapters, with the first ten hours timed. Underhand work and an obstacle race raise the stakes before the cup run.
52777-alaska-its-southern-coast-and-the-:
Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore wrote Alaska, a book on the southern coast and the Sitkan islands, with a map and pictures. A map by W H Dall, dated eighteen eighty-four, faces the title page. Scidmore quotes William H Seward on the wealth of the region.

Seward held that southern Alaska beat Germany in climate, soil, woods, and mines. The book treats the coast towns, the islands, and the people who lived there. It served as one volume in a set of short histories for general readers. Scidmore writes as a traveller who knew the north Pacific well. Clear detail makes the book a useful early guide.
52805-where-the-phph-pebbles-go:
Miriam Allen DeFord wrote a tale of a stone game on a far, dire world. The tale ran in Worlds of Tomorrow in April 1963. Gral and Hodnuth play phph, a game of lobbed stones. Stones are thrown at a mark as far off as skill lets. Each throw is then checked by a flight to the spot.

A good player wins heavy work from the crowd who watch. Ground folk are too small and light to lift the stones. Yet they love the game and throng to each match. Stars of the game need do no work of their own at all. DeFord builds a sly world from one odd sport.
56409-historical-record-of-the-seventeen:
British Army orders of January 1, 1836 frame the hosted text, part of a set of regimental records. The orders call for a full account of each regiment, from its raising through its stations and fights. This volume gives that account for the Seventeenth Regiment of Light Dragoons.

Inside, the record lists battles, sieges, and other actions, with the names of officers and men killed or wounded. It also names men praised for brave conduct and notes badges or marks of honor the regiment was allowed to bear. The preface argues that such records spur young soldiers to match the deeds of those who served before them.
57585-george-washington-or-life-in-ameri:
George Washington, or Life in America One Hundred Years Ago, by John Abbott, was copyrighted in 1875 in New York as part of the American Pioneers and Patriots set. Abbott ranks Washington as the most famed of American patriots, as Columbus and La Salle were the most famed pioneers. The book uses Washington's life to show how Americans lived a century before.

Abbott claims that the world moved more in the last century than in the five before it. Washington's career, he says, shows the manners, joys, and griefs of the young nation in rare detail. As statesman, general, and good man, Washington stands, for Abbott, without a match. The praise is warm and meant for young readers at home and school.
57702-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Victor Hugo is a guide compiled by David Widger. It lists the Hugo books held by Project Gutenberg and gives the table of contents for each in turn. The great novels head the list, and the reader can pass from the contents of one volume to the next without opening each book apart.

Les Miserables comes first, in the translation by Isabel Hapgood, opening with the books of Fantine: A Just Man and The Fall. Notre-Dame de Paris, Toilers of the Sea, and Napoleon the Little stand beside the Memoirs, the Poems, and the Dramas. Hapgood's Les Miserables contents run from the bishop, Monseigneur Bienvenu, to Jean Valjean and little Gervais.
58410-a-little-girl-in-old-chicago:
A Little Girl in Old Chicago is a novel by Amanda M Douglas, published by Dodd, Mead and Company of New York in 1904. It belongs to the author's Little Girl series, which visited old New York, Boston, Philadelphia, and other cities. The tale looks back at early Chicago through one child's life.

The narrator, Norman Hayne, remembers in his old age. Sunset over the lake opens his memory of the log house with its frame addition. Chapters follow the little girl through winter, dinners, and a political difference. Norman leaves and, much later, comes home. Polly and Dan carry the middle of the story. Wedding bells sound, and rivals appear. The last chapter is called The Passing of Old Chicago. Douglas wrote history as family memory, letting a growing city be measured by one household's years.
58707-kirsteen-the-story-of-a-scotch-fam:
Oliphant wrote Kirsteen, the story of a Scotch family seventy years before, and this is the first volume of the Tauchnitz edition. Bernhard Tauchnitz of Leipzig issued it in 1891 as volume 2719 of his Collection of British Authors. A long list of her other books faces the title, from the Chronicles of Carlingford to Hester and The Wizard's Son.

She inscribed the book, with love and respect, to Christina Rogerson. The tale opens with a question called through a house: where is Kirsteen? The answer comes in Scots, and canna tell you sets the tongue of the story. Kirsteen is the daughter at the center of a family in the Scotland of some 70 years before the writing. Readers get a family tale of duty and pride, told in the Scots voice Oliphant handled so well.
59020-fifty-years-ago:
Walter Besant wrote Fifty Years Ago, for Harper at New York. The book is profusely illustrated, its title page promises. A plate shows the Princess Victoria in 1830, from a Windsor picture. Besant had written All Sorts and Conditions of Men before it. James Rice had been his partner in a shelf of novels.

His desire in these pages, he writes, is to present a picture. The picture is of society in this country when the Queen ascended the throne. Streets, dress, amusements, and manners of that day fill the canvas. The book looks back half a century from its own season of change. Coaches, crinolines, and old London rise in its plates and text. Besant writes as a novelist turned witness of a vanished world. The volume gives 1837 England for the readers of a new age.
59348-life-on-the-congo:
Life on the Congo is a missionary account by Holman Bentley of the Baptist Mission. The Religious Tract Society published it in London. Grenfell, explorer of the upper Congo, wrote the introduction. A plate shows a cataract of the Congo from a mission station. The contents list eight chapters after that introduction. The Discovery of the Congo opens the narrative part. The Physical Features of the Congo follows as chapter two. Vegetation, climate, and people are treated in chapter three.

Home Life on the Congo gives the domestic picture in chapter four. The religious ideas of the native peoples come next. A chapter treats charms and secret societies among them. Missions in Central Africa and on the Congo River close the book. Grenfell notes that four years had sped since the chapters were penned. Events had followed each other fast in that brief interval.
59414-shango:
Shango, by John Jakes, ran in Worlds of If in February 1956. The headnote sets the puzzle: Valaya was a primitive society, yet its natives had a way of talking over distance that stumped the experts. Chief Van Isaac opens the tale at a wall-sized star map.

Van Isaac jabs a rodlike finger at a violet dot on the map and calls Valaya the new trouble spot. Arnold Koven, a lean man of thirty, has seen the telefilms scream of revolution for two weeks. Tribe fights tribe in slaughter, the reports said. Van Isaac fills in the past: folk from the Caribbean settled Valaya in the colonization. Sixty years of intermarriage added a slight blue Martian strain. Sugar and tin support the planet, left backward by its settlers' own choice. Raids from the small north continent drive the plot.
60095-croatian-tales-of-long-ago:
Ivana Brlic-Mazuranic wrote Croatian Tales of Long Ago, in her own tongue. Copeland translated the tales for Stokes at New York. Kirin drew the illustrations for the English edition. How Quest Sought the Truth opens the contents. Fisherman Plunk and his wife follow in the list of tales.

Reygoch, and Bridesman Sun and Bride Bridekins, stand in the contents. Stribor's Forest and a tale of Primrose and Lavender close it. Notes end the volume for English readers. Once an old man lived in a glade in an ancient forest. Witting was his name, and three grandsons lived with him. He had been father and mother to them, it says. Now they stood up to their grandfather's shoulder. All three brothers knew every pathway in the woods well. Brlic-Mazuranic gives Croatia a fairy book of its own.
60466-victor-hugo:
Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote Victor Hugo, issued at New York in 1886 by Worthington Company. A table of contents in French heads the book. The Work of Victor Hugo and La Legende des Siecles frame the essay. Swinburne opens with a sharp contrast between two springs more than two centuries apart.

In spring 1616 the greatest Englishman died with no public homage, Swinburne says. First tributes came seven years later in a garbled edition by two players, he notes. In spring 1885 the greatest Frenchman died amid universal anguish, he says. The gap is not wholly due to human progress in two hundred and sixty nine years, he holds. Nor is it due to French gratitude alone, he adds. Hugo was more than a poet, he argues. He was a healer, a comforter, a redeemer, and a prophet to his people.
62008-notes-upon-indigo:
Notes Upon Indigo, by John Hayes, treats the great blue dye stuff. The Press of John Wilson at Boston issued the notes in eighteen seventy three. Hayes was secretary of the National Association of Wool Manufacturers then. The piece first ran in the Bulletin of that wool trade body.

Hayes argues a wool journal must not neglect its secondary materials of trade. The hue the dyer gives is the charm of the largest fabric class. Indigo ranks with madder as one of the two chief dye stuffs of old. New chemical colours have lately forced indigo to give way in use. Hayes trusts a wiser economy and calmer taste will restore its place.
65360-charlie-and-his-puppy-bingo:
Helen Hill and Violet Maxwell wrote Charlie and His Puppy Bingo, a second book of Charlie stories printed at New York in 1923 and illustrated by the authors. They also wrote Charlie and His Kitten Topsy. Contents open with Bingo coming to live with Charlie and Charlie learning the traffic laws on the road.

How Bingo lost his spots, a ride on a real train's engine, Bingo and the angry rooster, and delivering mail for the stage driver follow. Charlie makes a pool and sails his boat, builds a real house out of brick, and teaches Bingo to come when called. A rainy day chapter closes the contents for young readers. Charlie lived with his mother, daddy, and auntie. Children got the puppy book.
66137-the-lost-ego:
Rog Phillips wrote The Lost Ego, a tale in a magazine of April 1953. Its hero knows he exists, and even knows his own name. But to really exist, the blurb says, a man has to have a body. His trouble is that he cannot find his. The tale opens in a living room with a strange woman raging at him.

She sneers that he spent the week's household money getting drunk last night. For a second he felt that she was his wife. Yet he had never seen her before in his life. His own voice startles him, quiet, calm, and patient. It sounds like a hold-up man he heard at six years old, in a store. That man shot a woman before his eyes in the memory. Phillips builds a tale of a mind adrift in the wrong life.
66472-a-letter-from-the-fire-being-an-ac:
Thomas D Foster writes home about the Great Chicago Fire in a letter dated October 31, 1871. The Torch Press of Cedar Rapids printed it in 1923. The printing was private. A photograph of Foster in London, Canada, fronts the page.

His son T Henry Foster offers the letter from Ottumwa, Iowa, in October 1923. Foster opens with shame at his long silence. The office still has no desks and no heat. He mulls over the fire while rain beats down. His tale starts on Saturday, October 7. He saw Mr Ackroyd off to Milwaukee. That night, at ten, a glare lit the sky as he reached his hotel. He watched the firemen play water on the crowd. Such letters fix the great fire in one man's plain words.
66485-nick-carter-stories-no-134-april-3:
Nick Carter Stories number 134, dated April 3, 1915, is a weekly dime novel from Street and Smith of New York, priced at five cents. The story, The Secret of Shangore, or Nick Carter among the Spearmen, is billed as edited by Chickering Carter. It opens by a camp fire in a strange land beyond the Himalayas.

Millionaire shipowner Jefferson Arnold vows to catch the crook William Pike and to free his son Leslie, held among spearmen in a country few white men leave alive. Carter calmly agrees to push on. The number is pure pulp: fast talk, exotic danger, and a hero who never doubts.
67378-john-solomon-supercargo:
Allan Hawkwood, the pen name of Henry Bedford-Jones, wrote John Solomon, Supercargo, issued in London in 1925. The tale opens at the cattle-wharf at Deptford, where Viscount Ratcliff strolls in yachting dress. Harcourt looks out of place among the cattle hands, yet his brown face and broad frame win respect. A foul, rag-clad hand on a worn cargo ship calls down to him, and the plot begins.

Chapter names point to a road to Melindi, a murder charge, and a place of skulls. A lady professor, Dr. Krausz, and a ship named Daphne all play parts. Solomon plans and acts while others fall under doubt. Readers get a brisk sea tale of crime, trade, and far ports.
6750-the-hawaiian-archipelago:
Isabella Bird spent nearly seven months in Hawaii, traveling for health, and wrote these letters to her sister, to whom the book is dedicated. She landed by chance, found the climate a benefit, and stayed to ride horseback through the isles, climb mountains, visit active volcanoes, and reach remote regions. Open air and exercise were her cure.

Palm groves, coral reefs, and volcanoes of the Sandwich Islands fill her letters, with keen notes on people, plants, and daily life. Bird writes with a traveler's vigor and a woman's frank eye. The Hawaiian Archipelago is a classic, delightful travel book, still fresh after more than a century.
68450-easy-come-easy-go:
Easy Come, Easy Go is a western novel by Edwin Sabin, author of The Devil of the Picuris. A notice at the front calls it a delightful story of a real Westerner, set down in engaging fashion. The tale opens at a beef round-up camp in the last stages of the trail drive. At noon, as the cook yells for the men to come and get it, a buckboard drives in across the brown, parched plains.

In it ride a stout ruddy man, a younger man, and two dazzling girls dressed for the Wild West. Lengthy Tex, foreman of the 77 outfit, rises to meet them. The owner from the East has come to see his own cows and men, and his guests stare open-eyed at the punchers eating. It is one world laid over another.
68894-twenty-tales-by-twenty-women-from-:
Twenty Tales by Twenty Women is a book of tales said to be from real life in Chicago, put out in that city in nineteen hundred and three with all rights held. No name stands on the title leaf for the whole. A short first part and a brief set of first words lead in. Then the tales come one by one, each with its own name in the list of parts.

The names of the tales tell the span of the book. A diary of a Chicago girl stands first. A life tale of a south land widow comes next. A tale of the poor Jews' ward of the town comes next in line. A woman of eight and thirty years and a proud house of Kentucky fill the first half.
69316-letters-of-a-japanese-schoolboy-ha:
Wallace Irwin wrote these comic letters of Hashimura Togo, a Japanese schoolboy in America. Doubleday, Page printed the book at New York in 1909, with Rollin Kirby's drawings. The pieces had run in Collier's through 1907 and 1908.

Therefore I entertain him to beer-ceremony at the saloon of the honourable Strunsky, Irish patriot: a Kirby plate line shows the whole method. Togo writes home in broken, bright English on all he meets. Our Noble Allies, the Honourable War Cloud, and the Yellow Peril open the set. Lady suffragettes, money panics, and the simple life among ambassadors follow. A third term for our emperor and plain talk on race stand in the list. Its jokes cut several ways at once.
72002-christmas-in-chicago:
Fanny Butcher wrote Christmas in Chicago, a bright sketch of the city at the feast. Houghton Mifflin issued the book in Boston and New York in nineteen hundred twenty six. Theresa Garrett Eliot drew the pictures for it. A giant town tree on the lake front opens the scene.

Its star shames the mild stars in the blue black sky. Throngs tramp in snow below to a band’s loud strains. Heilige Nacht swells while car horns honk past in streams. Faces from all the earth mix in the press of folk. Small kin trees gleam down miles of parks and broad roads. Steel mills paint the south sky flame red at dusk. North suburbs rest in calm past the last small tree. Butcher paints the whole town as one vast Christmas house.
73301-four-girls-of-forty-years-ago:
Four Girls of Forty Years Ago is a girls' story by Nina Rhoades. Lothrop, Lee and Shepard published it at Boston in 1920. Eleanor Weeden illustrated the volume. Rhoades wrote other girls' books, including Dorothy Brown and Victorine's Book. The book also belongs to the Brick House series for younger readers. That series holds titles like Only Dollie and Little Miss Rosamond. The frontispiece shows a girl praising a wonderful person.

The title sets the tale forty years before its readers' day. Four girls stand at the centre of the story. The publisher's list prices the book for young girl readers. Its companions stress home, neighbours, and small adventures. The cover art of a brick house marks the series at a glance.
73398-travels-in-the-east-indian-archipe:
Albert Bickmore sailed to the East Indian Archipelago to re-collect the shells pictured in Rumphius's old book of Amboina rarities. His Travels, printed by John Murray at London in 1868, tells the whole voyage. Bickmore was a professor of natural history, and the Dutch government, far from blocking him, gave him leave to roam the Spice Islands and gather specimens. His route took him through Batavia and across the archipelago, from Java toward the Moluccas.

The narrative comes almost wholly from the journal he kept day by day, and he aimed at accuracy over elegance. Harbors, peoples, markets, fevers, and butterflies all find their place, beside the shells that were the errand of the trip. The book is a working naturalist's record of the islands as he passed through them.
76669-plan-of-chicago:
Plan of Chicago is a city planning report by Daniel Burnham and Edward Bennett, architects. The Commercial Club of Chicago published it in 1909. It was prepared under the club's direction during 1906, 1907, and 1908. Charles Moore edited the volume for the club. A frontispiece shows Chicago in bird's eye view on Lake Michigan's shore. Jules Guerin painted that view for the Commercial Club. The smaller towns around the city appear tied by radiating roads. The contents open with the origin of the plan.

That chapter treats the tendency toward city life first. The problems of the great city follow in its heads. The necessity for city planning is argued next. Economy and efficiency are promoted by a city plan, it holds. The elements of a comprehensive plan are then set out. The Burnham Plan became a landmark of American city planning.
76799-a-girl-s-life-eighty-years-ago:
A Girl's Life Eighty Years Ago prints selections from the letters of Eliza Southgate Bowne. Clarence Cook wrote the introduction. Scribner's published the book in New York in 1887. Portraits and views illustrate the letters. A miniature of the writer forms the frontispiece.

Eliza Southgate was born at Scarborough, Maine, in 1783. She was the third of twelve children. Her father was a doctor of English stock. He rode into Scarborough with his goods in saddle-bags. He picked up law as well as medicine. In time he won a good position in the town. The letters show a girl's life in the early republic. The illustrations add the houses and kin of her world. Rufus King and the Bowne house at Flushing appear.
7988-a-thousand-and-one-afternoons-in-ch:
Ben Hecht collected these newspaper sketches of Chicago, written for the Chicago Daily News, into a book whose preface recalls a rainy spring day in 1921. Hecht had left the staff for publicity work, found the pay good and the luncheons endless, and came back sullen to the editorial coop. The pieces that follow wander the city in the manner of Scheherazade: a thousand and one afternoons, each with its own characters, from street corners to courtrooms.

Hecht's Chicago is vivid, cynical, and tender by turns, and his prose made him famous. The sketches show a city of hustlers, dreamers, and ordinary people caught in extraordinary moments. As journalism turned literature, the book remains a landmark of American city writing and a portrait of Chicago in the Jazz Age.
8641-sketches-from-concord-and-appledore:
Frank Preston Stearns recalls Concord, Massachusetts, as it was a generation earlier, and the writers who made the town famous. Separate sketches cover Nathaniel Hawthorne, Louisa M. Alcott, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Matthew Arnold on his lecture visit, David A. Wasson, and Wendell Phillips. A final section moves to Appledore, the island home of the Laighton family, and its visitor John Greenleaf Whittier.

Stearns writes as a neighbour remembering faces, talk, and habits, not as a critic judging books. The sketches preserve small details: how Emerson spoke, how Hawthorne kept his distance, how Alcott's household ran. For readers of American literature, the book offers a warm, firsthand gallery of Concord's golden age, seen from inside the town rather than from a library shelf.
a-frog-he-would-a-wooing-go: Randolph Caldecott illustrates the old song of a frog who would go wooing. The frog sets off in his opera hat and meets a rat on the way. Together they go to see pretty Miss Mousey, with a rowley powley chorus. Caldecott's pictures make the nursery rhyme a delight for children.
a-thousand-and-one-afternoons-in-chicago: Ben Hecht gathers a thousand and one afternoons in Chicago in this volume, prefaced by a spring day in 1921 in the Chicago Daily News editorial coop. Hecht walks in, divorced from the staff for some weeks and married to an overdressed, blatant creature called Publicity. The pay is preposterous, the luncheons limitless, the work easy and the taxis plenteous. Yet he cannot stand another luncheon, and the sketches that follow return him to the city's streets.
as-we-go:
Charles Dudley Warner gathered twenty-eight short studies in this companion volume to As We Were Saying, drawn like it from his newspaper writing. The contents range over the whole surface of American life in the 1890s. Our President, the first piece, opens by asking how kings got started and what election does to privilege.

The rest follow his columnist's beat in no order but curiosity. The newspaper-made man, interesting girls, the tall girl, and the whistling girl treat the types of the day. Weather and character, climate and happiness, the art of idleness, and the deadly diary treat its habits. Warner's touch is light and his sentences short; these are essays to be taken one at a sitting, like the columns they were.
britannica-1911-abednego: Abednego is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the name as the Babylonian name laid on Azariah, one of Daniel's companions, citing the first chapter of Daniel. The name is likely a corruption, perhaps a deliberate one, of Abednebo, servant of Nebo, the entry holds. G Hoffmann's rival reading, Abednergal, servant of the god Nergal, is also set down. C H Toy's link to Barnebo, son of Nebo, closes the note, with Barnabas named as a veiled form of the same name.
britannica-1911-antigo: Antigo is a city and county seat of Langlade County in Wisconsin in this short 1911 Britannica place note. It stands far north west of Milwaukee on a rail line. Its folk count rose to seven thousand one hundred ninety six by nineteen ten. Farm and wood lands round it feed its trade and mills. Saws, chairs, tables, doors, and wheel parts are its chief made goods. First homes rose in eighteen eighty, and city rank came five years on. Its name springs from an Indian word for evergreen.
britannica-1911-baringo:
Baringo is a lake of British East Africa, some thirty miles north of the equator in the eastern rift valley. It is one of a chain of lakes studding the valley floor, at 3,325 feet above the sea. About sixteen miles long by nine broad, it has an irregular outline, its northern shore deeply indented, and its waters are brackish.

Several small streams feed the lake, but it has no outlet. South of it lies a flat, marshy, fertile grain country, home of the Njamusi, described as peaceful farmers friendly to Europeans. The 1911 Britannica entry notes the Karosi hills to the north and terraces rising east to the Laikipia escarpment. A local oddity is the termite hills, hollow columns ten to twelve feet high.
britannica-1911-barocci-federigo:
Federigo Barocci (1528–1612) was an Italian painter, born at Urbino, where the genius of Raphael inspired him. In his early youth he travelled to Rome, painted in fresco there, and was warmly commended by Michelangelo. Then he returned to Urbino and, apart from short visits to Rome, lived there until his death.

Barocci won great fame by his paintings of religious subjects, and in style he imitated Correggio to some extent. His followers were very numerous, though Lanzi's history of painting holds that they carried their master's peculiarities to excess. The 1911 Britannica entry adds a second craft: Barocci etched a few prints from his own designs, highly finished and worked with great softness and delicacy.
britannica-1911-barugo: Barugo is a town on the north coast of Leyte province, on the island of Leyte in the Philippine Islands, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on Carigara Bay, facing the sea on the island's northern shore. Its population in the 1903 count was 12,360. Trade is the town's other recorded feature. Barugo exported large quantities of hemp and copra, the dried flesh of the coconut used for oil. It brought in rice, petroleum, and cotton goods from outside.
britannica-1911-belgian-congo: Belgian Congo names a Belgian colony in Equatorial Africa that held the greater part of the basin of the Congo river. Before that it was the Independent State of the Congo, often called the Congo Free State. Belgium annexed the territory in 1908, and this short entry simply records that change of rule and points readers to the Congo Free State article for the fuller account.
britannica-1911-bogo: Bogo is the subject of a short town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bogo is a town in the province of Cebu, on the island of Cebu in the Philippine Islands. It stands on Bogo Bay at the mouth of the Bulac river. By 1903 its people numbered near fifteen thousand. The climate is hot but healthy. The land around is fertile and yields sugar, corn, and maguey in plenty. Rice, cacao, and fruits are also grown. Hats, baskets, cloth, and rope are woven for export.
britannica-1911-boito-arrigo:
Arrigo Boito (born 1842) was an Italian poet and composer who split his life between words and music. Born at Padua, he studied at the Milan Conservatoire, yet spent as much time on literature as on music even there. With Franco Faccio he wrote a cantata, Le Sorelle d'Italia, that was performed with success.

After years of travel he settled in Milan, wrote journalism, and fought under Garibaldi in 1866. His opera Mefistofele failed outright at La Scala in 1868 and was pulled after two nights. Cut down and reworked, it triumphed at Bologna in 1875 and played London in 1880. The entry praises his Faust for standing closer to Goethe than Gounod's version, while noting it never quite won a firm popular place.
britannica-1911-calderon-rodrigo:
Rodrigo Calderón (d. 1621) was a Spanish court favourite and adventurer. He held the titles of count of Oliva and marquis de las Siete Iglesias. This 1911 Britannica entry tells his rise and ruin. He was born at Antwerp, of mixed Spanish and Flemish parentage. In 1598 he entered the service of the duke of Lerma. Lerma ruled Spain through his hold on Philip III.

Calderón made himself Lerma's trusted agent. He was active, able and unscrupulous. Titles, offices and plunder flowed to him fast. His greed and insolence made him widely hated. Enemies worked through Queen Margarita against him. He lost the secretaryship in 1611, but kept Lerma's favour. In 1614 he became marquis de las Siete Iglesias. When the queen died, some accused him of witchcraft against her. The entry follows the charges that gathered around him.
britannica-1911-cargo:
Cargo is the load carried on board a ship. The word is Spanish for “loading.” It comes from the Latin carrus, meaning a car. This very short 1911 Britannica entry defines the term. A cargo is a shipload, in the strict sense. It may also mean the goods carried on board. Less technically, it can even cover persons carried. By analogy it serves for any large amount of anything.

The entry gives no law of its own here. The maritime law of cargo is dealt with elsewhere. It points readers to the articles on Average and Affreightment. Insurance, Salvage, Bottomry and Lien are also named. The special ships built for cargo are treated under Ship. The whole notice is a few lines long. It gives the meaning and the cross-references, and nothing more.
britannica-1911-cartago:
Cartago is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the capital of the province of Cartago in Costa Rica, Central America. It lies 13 miles east-south-east of San José on the trans-continental railway, and its population in 1900 was 4536. The town is built 4930 feet above sea level on the plateau of San José, at the southern base of the volcano Irazú, which rises to 11,200 feet. Hot mineral springs at the suburb of Bella Vista draw many invalids.

Disaster marks the town's older buildings, above all its churches. In 1723 the flooded crater of Irazú burst and nearly overwhelmed Cartago, and an earthquake shattered it in 1841. Local trade rests chiefly on fine coffee grown in the rich volcanic soil. The town may date to 1522 and kept its rank as Costa Rica's capital until 1823. After the government moved to San José its prosperity faded, then partly revived as railways spread after 1871.
britannica-1911-ciudad-rodrigo:
Ciudad Rodrigo is a town of western Spain in Salamanca, eight miles east of the Portuguese frontier, on the right bank of the Agueda. Its people numbered 8,930 in 1900, and the Salamanca to Coimbra railway serves it. The town is an episcopal see and was for centuries an important frontier fortress. Its cathedral dates from 1190 but was restored in the 15th century.

Remains of a Roman aqueduct and bridge foundations suggest a Roman settlement stood on the site first. Count Rodrigo Gonzalez founded the town in the 12th century, and its name derives from his. During the Peninsular War the French under Marshal Ney captured it in 1810. Wellington retook it on 19 January 1812 and was created duke of Ciudad Rodrigo for that exploit, among other new titles.
britannica-1911-clemencin-diego:
Clemencin, Diego is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Spanish scholar and public man. He was born on the twenty-seventh of September 1765 at Murcia and died in 1834. He was schooled there, then gave up the plan of taking orders. In 1788 he found work at Madrid as tutor to the sons of a countess-duchess.

He gave himself to the study of old remains. In 1807 he became editor of the Gaceta de Madrid. The next year Murat sentenced him to death for a piece, and he fled to Cadiz. Under the central junta he held posts, then lost them in the reaction of 1814. In the liberal years 1820 to 1823 he served as colonial minister, then faced exile till 1827. In 1833 he brought out the first volume of his great edition of Don Quixote.
britannica-1911-colugo: Colugo is a short animal article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about either of two species of the genus Galeopithecus. The animals live in the forests of the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Borneo and the Philippines, feeding chiefly on leaves. About the size of cats, they have long slender limbs joined by a broad fold of skin, with webbed fingers and toes. By day they cling head downwards to tree trunks in rest. At night they glide from tree to tree on the skin parachute.
britannica-1911-delmedigo:
Delmedigo is the subject of a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Delmedigo was a Cretan Jewish family. The article treats its two most important members in turn. The first is Elijah Delmedigo, a thinker who lived from 1460 to 1497. He taught in several centres of learning in Italy. At the urging of Pico della Mirandola he translated works of Averroes into Latin.

In matters of faith, Elijah marks a move away from the school view that faith and thought are one and the same. His most important work was devoted to that inquiry into religion. The second figure is Joseph Solomon Delmedigo, who lived from 1591 to 1655. He was a pupil of Galileo and wrote many books on science and thought. He bore a large part in starting a critical movement in Judaism.
britannica-1911-embargo:
Embargo, a Spanish word meaning “stoppage,” is in international law the holding by a state of vessels within its ports as a measure of public good. In practice it serves as a way of pressing a weaker state. The entry quotes Magna Carta of 1215 on foreign merchants found in the land at a war's start.

Embargoes in advance of war have long fallen out of use, the entry says. On a war's outbreak, enemies now often grant trading vessels a delay to leave port, so neither ship nor cargo faces seizure. A Hague Convention of 1907 confirmed that practice. A merchant ship of one belligerent caught in an enemy port should be let to depart freely, at once or after days of grace. A ship that cannot leave may only be detained, not seized, and must be restored after the war or paid for.
britannica-1911-fernandez-diego:
Diego Fernandez, a Spanish adventurer and historian of the sixteenth century, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Palencia and schooled for the church. About 1545 he sailed for Peru, where he served in the royal army. The viceroy of Peru made him chronicler of that land in 1555.

In that post Fernandez wrote a narrative of the revolt of Francisco Hernandez Giron and the rebellion of Gonzalo Pizarro. He also covered the rule of Pedro de la Gasca, who restored royal order. The whole work came out at Seville in 1571, dedicated to King Philip the Second. The entry praises its clear, plain style and its wealth of detail. He had access to the letters and official papers of the Spanish leaders. With that bias noted, it is the fullest and most trusted record of the events it tells.
britannica-1911-flamingo:
The flamingo is among the tallest and most beautiful of birds, marked by a bright flame-coloured or scarlet patch on its wings. Long known by its classical name Phoenicopterus, it lives around most countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea. Its range is very wide, yet the single genus holds only a few species. The rosy Phoenicopterus roseus runs from the Cape Verde Islands to India and Ceylon, and north to Lake Baikal.

Other species fill out the map in the entry. The vermilion P. ruber spreads from Florida to Para and the Galapagos, P. chilensis from Peru to Patagonia, and the tallest, P. andinus, haunts the salt lakes of the Atacama desert. Fossil flamingos from France and Oregon show the family is old. Earlier fossil kin had shorter legs and longer toes, a less specialized build than the long-legged birds of today.
britannica-1911-foscolo-ugo:
Ugo Foscolo (1778-1827), Italian writer, was born at Zante in the Ionian Isles on 26 January 1778. His father, a physician at Spalatro in Dalmatia, died while he was young, and the family moved to Venice. At the University of Padua he continued studies begun in a Dalmatian grammar school. Among his Paduan masters was the abbe Cesarotti, whose version of Ossian had made that work popular in Italy. That master shaped Foscolo's tastes, and his knowledge of modern languages eased his Greek studies.

Foscolo's ambition showed itself in 1797 with his tragedy Tieste, which won a measure of success. He had changed his Christian name from Niccolo to Ugo, for reasons not clearly explained. He now threw himself into the stormy political debates of the revolutionary years in Italy. The long entry follows the poet of the Sepolcri and the novelist of Jacopo Ortis through exile and his last years in England.
britannica-1911-fusaro-lago: Fusaro, Lago, is a lake of Campania in Italy, west of Baia and south of the acropolis of Cumae, held to be the ancient Acherusia palus. A line of sandhills cuts it off from the sea, and it may have served as the harbour of Cumae in early antiquity. In the first century A.D. an artificial outlet was dug at its south end, running through a tunnel under the hill of Torregaveta. Villas stood on its shores, and oyster growing continues there.
britannica-1911-galago:
Galago is the Senegal name, now the technical one, for the long-tailed African members of the lemur-like primates. Galagos are classed with the lorises and pottos in the family Nycticebidae, marked by the lengthened upper part of the foot and by ears that fold. They live through most of Africa south of the Sahara, from Senegambia to Abyssinia and down to Natal, in the wooded districts. By day they sleep; at night they grow active, feeding on fruits, insects and small birds.

On the ground they sit upright and jump with their hind legs like jerboas. They are pretty animals, from the size of a small cat down to less than a rat, with large eyes and ears, soft woolly fur and long tails. The largest species, G. crassicaudatus of Mozambique, heads the Otolemur group, while G. senegalensis of Senegal stands for the typical group.
britannica-1911-giambelli-federigo:
Federigo Giambelli, an Italian army engineer of the 1500s, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Mantua near the mid 1500s. After work in Italy he went to Spain to offer his skill to Philip the Second. The king gave him a cool welcome and no post at once.

Giambelli settled at Antwerp and won a name for wide science there. When Parma besieged the town in 1584, he vowed revenge on Spain. Queen Elizabeth hired him to aid the town's defense. Two of his ships were turned into blast craft and blew a great breach in the bridge. Later he worked on the Thames walls in England. His death year is not known.
britannica-1911-gogo: Gogo, also spelled Gogha, is a small port town in British India in the 1911 Britannica. It lies in the Ahmedabad district of Bombay, north west of Bombay city. Its folk count for nineteen oh one was four thousand seven hundred ninety eight. A safe road for ships lies east of town, kept calm by Piram Island. Local men were famed as the best sailors in India. The town lost trade and shrank after its peak as a cotton mart in the years of the American Civil War.
britannica-1911-gomez-diogo:
Gomez, Diogo is an explorer article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Portuguese seaman and writer of the fifteenth century. Gomez appears first as a knight of the royal household and customs receiver at Cintra. His lasting value is his Latin chronicle, written for Martin Behaim, of the life and discoveries of Prince Henry the Navigator. It falls into three parts, on Guinea, on the western islands, and on the Azores.

The article explains why the chronicle matters. It is the only contemporary account of the rediscovery of the Azores. Gomez tells of his own voyage past Cape Verde to the Gambia river. The article draws on his descriptions of the Niger gold trade.
britannica-1911-hiogo:
Hiogo is a town of Japan in the province of Settsu, on the west shore of the bay of Osaka. The 1911 Britannica article says it stands next to the foreign settlement of Kobe, twenty-one miles west of Osaka. Its growth had been swift and striking. The count of Hiogo with Kobe rose from 135,639 in 1891 to 285,002 in 1903. Trade grew near eightfold in the last years of the century.

Silk and cotton cloth, floor mats, straw plaits, matches, and cotton yarns lead its trade. Kobe serves in large part as the shipping port of Osaka, the chief mill town of Japan. Foreigners there pass one thousand, apart from the Chinese. The air is praised as pure and dry, the best of the treaty ports. Wharves take large steamers, and a shipyard and docks stand near by.
britannica-1911-jingo:
Jingo is an article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica with two subjects under one name. The first Jingo is a legendary empress of Japan, wife of the mikado Chuai. On her husband's death she took up the rule herself. She fitted out an army and led an invasion of Korea.

The entry says she returned home in full victory after three years. Her son, born later, was in time worshipped as Hachiman, god of war. Jingo is said to have ruled Japan until the year 270 and is still worshipped. The article then turns to the English oath By Jingo. Its origin is called doubtful, and several guesses are weighed. One links it to a Burgundian saint, another to a Basque name for God. The piece shows how one short word can carry a legend and a catchphrase at once.
britannica-1911-jones-inigo:
Inigo Jones, an English architect who lived from 1573 to 1651, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is at times called the English Palladio. Born in London, the son of a cloth worker, he first trained with a joiner. His gift for drawing won him patrons who sent him to study in Italy.

In Italy his love moved from landscape painting to building design. He worked in the style of Palladio and won such fame that the king of Denmark called him north. He then joined the court of James the First in England. Jones designed court masques and became surveyor general of royal buildings. He drew plans for a new palace at Whitehall. Work on Saint Pauls and a clash with Ben Jonson over the masques are also noted. He died in poverty after the Civil War.
britannica-1911-kollontaj-hugo:
Hugo Kollontaj (1750–1812) was a Polish politician and writer, born at Niecislawice in Sandomir and educated at Pinczow and Cracow. He took orders, went to Rome in 1770 and gained degrees in theology and common law, with a strong taste for art. Back in Poland he threw himself into school reform. He reshaped the university of Cracow to his own plan and was its rector from 1782 to 1785, against much clerical resistance.

In 1786 Kollontaj became referendarius of Lithuania. During the Four Years' Diet (1788–1792) he stood at the head of the reform party and drove the work that produced the constitution of the 3rd of May 1791. He became vice-chancellor that June. When the reaction won, he fled to Dresden. He returned for Kosciuszko's rising and served as finance minister, but his radical views set him against the dictator himself.
britannica-1911-mago:
Mago is a name held by more than one man of Carthage in this 1911 Britannica past entry. The first is said to have built the war power of that city. The best known is the young son of Hamilcar Barca. He marched with his brother Hannibal into Italy in the great war. He held chief posts in the wins of the first three years.

After Cannae he sailed home to tell of the wins in the field. Orders sent him to Spain to aid his kin there in place of Italy. Beat in Spain, he held Gades for a time, then took the war to Liguria. Beat once more, he died of wounds on the sail home. A third Mago wrote a great work on farm craft, kept as a norm by Rome.
britannica-1911-new-siberia-archipelago:
The New Siberia Archipelago is a group of islands off the Arctic coast of Siberia. The name is loosely used, the entry warns at the start. It may cover the northern group of islands only, in strict use. It may also be stretched to cover a southern group, the Lyakhov Islands. Doubt also hangs over three islands found by the Jeannette expedition far to the north.

One of those three islands belongs by land form to the New Siberia group. The other two lie too far away to count as part of it. Land due north of Kotelnyi Island has been sighted but not settled. The main group runs from Kotelnyi in the west to New Siberia in the east. Kotelnyi is the largest island, one hundred sixteen miles long. A small island lies near its western shore in the sea.
britannica-1911-owego: Owego is a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on a village in New York state. It is the seat of Tioga county, on the north side of the Susquehanna river. The census of 1910 counted a little over four thousand six hundred people. Three rail lines serve the village. It stands on the site of an old Indian village named Ah-wa-ga, razed in 1779. The name is said to mean where the valley widens. A white trading post rose there in 1785.
britannica-1911-park-mungo:
Mungo Park was a Scots man who traced the great stream of west Africa, and lived from seventeen seventy-one to past eighteen five. He was born on a farm in the south of Scotland, one of thirteen young. He was trained as a cut healer, took a degree, and sailed past the chief isles as aid on a trade ship.

He gave his aid to a guild that sought the course of the great stream, past the death of its last man. He sailed to a post on a small stream and set out for the wild lands with two aids. A chief held him in chains for four months. He fled with naught but his horse and a small tool, and at last saw the great stream.
britannica-1911-plumbago:
Plumbago is an old name for graphite, the stuff of pencil leads. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes the word from the Latin for lead. The stone looks a bit like lead, which won it the name black lead. It once had a name in medicine as a cure. By 1911 it was held to have no healing worth at all. The hosted text reaches the entry after the tail of a piece on plum disease.

A linked sense of the word names a kind of drawing. What we now call pencil drawings were once called plumbago drawings. That usage ruled in the 1600s and 1700s. Fine portrait sketches of that age often go by the term. The entry is short, and it points readers to the main graphite article for the stone itself. Its value lies in fixing two old uses of one word.
britannica-1911-rovigo:
Rovigo, a town in Venetia, Italy, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It is the capital of the province of the same name. The town stands on low ground between the lower Adige and the lower Po. It lies south west of Venice, above sea level by just a few feet.

Rail lines link it to Bologna, Padua, Legnago, and Chioggia. Its church of Santo Stefano dates from sixteen ninety six. A round church with a fine bell tower was begun in fifteen ninety four. The town hall holds a library with rare early books and a picture set. Two towers of the old castle still stand. Wool, silk, linen, and leather are made in the town.
britannica-1911-sago:
Sago, a food starch taken from the trunk of some palms, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The chief source is the sago palm, a tree of the East Indian islands, with whole forests of it on Ceram. The trees grow only in low, wet ground and reach full starch bearing age at about fifteen years.

At that age the trunk is packed with a soft, spongy core, held in by a hard rind. If the fruit is left to ripen, that core is used up and the tree dies at once. So ripe palms are cut, split, and the pith is grated to a powder. Workers knead the powder with water over a sieve, and the starch sinks in a trough. One or two washes leave it fit for cakes and soups. For export it is made into paste and rubbed through sieves into small grains.
britannica-1911-supercargo: Supercargo is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a post in sea trade law. The word comes from a Spanish term for a man set over a cargo. Cargo owners hire him to sail with the goods and run their trade. He sells the goods at each port and buys more for the trip home. He holds charge of the cargo unless his deal sets a limit. A factor, by contrast, stays fixed at one port.
britannica-1911-tierra-del-fuego:
Tierra del Fuego is a chain of isles at the south tip of South America, and the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica draws its bounds. A strait splits it from the main land. At its tight points that strait is scarce a mile wide. The group runs for past four hundred miles from north west to south east.

From west to east it runs for about two hundred and seventy miles. South it thins to half that breadth. Past its east point lies one last isle that ends in a cape of its own. The line that parts the lands of Argentina and Chile in this group has been set by pact. Argentina holds the part of the chief isle that lies east of a set line of the globe.
britannica-1911-tobago:
Tobago is an island article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an island in the British West Indies. It lies twenty miles north east of Trinidad. The island runs twenty six miles long and has an area of 114 square miles. Its count is given as 18,751.

The article describes one steep mass of old volcanic rock. The centre rises to 1,800 feet, and thick woods clothe much of the land. In the high Rain Preserve the trees may never be felled, to keep the rains coming. Heat holds near eighty one degrees all year. Farms yield rubber, cotton, sugar, coffee, cocoa, tobacco, and nutmegs for export. The capital, Scarborough, stands on the south coast. Columbus first sighted the island in 1498, and Britain took it for good in 1814.
capt-w-f-drannan-chief-of-scouts-as-pilo:
William F. Drannan told his own tale as chief of scouts on the plains, in a book of 1910. E. Bert Smith drew rich plates for it. The book stands as a mate to his Thirty One Years on the Plains and in the Mountains. Twelve chapters line the contents, named by count alone in the copy held here.
